title: A World of Objects
tagline: One character is lonely. Time to fill the screen.
newIdea: Lists and loops — handling many things at once
builtOn: Lesson 4 — your controllable character. Everything from Lessons 1–4 stays.
goals: Use a **counting** `for` loop to create a lot of things at once
Use a **for-each** loop to visit every thing in a list
Use `random()` to give a world variety

vocab.def: a list that holds many objects of the same type. It grows as you add more
repeats a block a set number of times. Used to **create** things
visits every item already in a list, one at a time. Used to **visit** things
an item's position in a list. Lists start counting at **0**, not 1

warmup: How do you make your character move toward the mouse? Where exactly does that call go, and why there?

p: Say you want twelve coins. You could write twelve variables: `coin1`, `coin2`, `coin3`… and then twelve `new Blob(...)` lines, and twelve `move()` calls, and twelve `drawSprite()` calls. That is thirty-six lines to manage, and if you want a thirteenth coin you write three more.
A list fixes that. Think of it as a **bag** — you keep stuffing things in, and the bag does not care how many.

code.label: Three things you do with a list
code.body:
ArrayList<Blob> coins;                 // 1. declare it (what kind of bag)
coins = new ArrayList<Blob>();        // 2. create it (get an empty bag)
coins.add(new Blob(...));             // 3. add to it (put something in)

p: Java uses the same word, `for`, for two loops that feel completely different. Keeping them straight is the real skill in this lesson.
This one counts. `i` starts at 0, and the loop repeats until `i` reaches 12. You use it in `setup()` to build your world.

code.label: "Do this 12 times"

bullets: `i < 12` — keep going while i is under 12
`i++` — add one to i each time around

p: This one does not count. It just walks the list and hands you one item at a time. You use it in `draw()` to move and draw everything.

code.label: "For each coin c in the list, do this"

howItWorks.h: You cannot call a method on the whole bag
p: This is the mistake almost everyone makes at least once:

code.label: Wrong, then right

bullets: The bag is not a coin. You cannot ask the bag to draw itself — you have to reach in and ask each coin.

howItWorks.h: Draw order decides what is on top
p: Whatever you draw **last** appears in front. That is why the player is drawn after the coins in the starter code — so your character is never hidden behind a coin.
This becomes a big deal in Lesson 8.

steps: Open your Lesson 4 sketch. Your `MyCharacter` tab still does not change.
At the top of the sketch, next to `MyCharacter player;`, declare the list: `ArrayList<Blob> coins;`
In `setup()`, create the empty list: `coins = new ArrayList<Blob>();`
Below that, add the counting loop from the starter code. Run it. Nothing shows up yet — you made the coins but never drew them.
In `draw()`, **above** your player lines, add the for-each loop that moves and draws each coin. Run again. Now the world is full.
Change the `12` in the counting loop to `40`. Run. Then try `3`. How many feels right?
Change the coin color to something that fits your character's world.
Move the player lines **above** the coin loop and run. Your character disappears behind the coins. Move them back. That is draw order.
Add a `mousePressed()` that spawns a new coin wherever you click: `coins.add(new Blob(this, mouseX, mouseY, 12, color(255, 220, 50)));`

makeItYours: Change the number of things in your world, their speed, and their size.
Change their color and shape so they belong in **your** world — gems, fish, stars, bubbles, asteroids, hearts.
Add a **second** `ArrayList` of a different kind of thing. Enemies? Stars in the background? Two lists means two loops in `draw()`.
Add a `mousePressed()` that spawns a new object wherever you click.
Make one list slow and drifting and another fast and darting — it makes the world feel layered.
challenge: Write your own environment sprite class in a new tab — a `Cloud`, a `Tree`, a `Star`. It is the same `extends Blob` pattern from Lesson 2. Then make an `ArrayList` of those and fill your world with them. There is a `Cloud` example above to start from.
flintHint: Good things to ask: "what is the difference between a counting for loop and a for-each loop?", "my coins are not showing up", or "how do I make a second list of a different color?" Paste in your `setup()` if something will not run.
wrapup: What is the difference between the counting `for` loop and the for-each loop? When would you use each one?
assignmentTask: Fill your character's world with things — created with a counting loop, drawn with a for-each loop.
assignmentDo: Declare an `ArrayList`, create it in `setup()`, and fill it with a **counting** loop.
Move and draw everything in it with a **for-each** loop in `draw()`.
Use `random()` so the objects are not all identical.
Make the world yours — the count, the colors, the sizes, and the speeds should say something about the game you are building.
Draw your player **last** so it appears on top.
submit: A screenshot or short recording of your populated world.
Your answer to **Show your thinking** below.
checklist: Use a **counting** `for` loop to make many objects.
Use a **for-each** loop to move and draw each one.
Explain the difference between the two loops.
standard: Store many objects in an `ArrayList` and process them with both loop styles; use `random()` for variety.

stages.name: Getting Started
stages.text: My list of objects is not appearing. **Next step:** **create** things with a counting loop in `setup()` (`for (int i ...)`) and **draw** them with a for-each loop in `draw()` (`for (Blob c : coins)`). Check that you call `drawSprite()` on each item `c`, not on the whole list.

stages.name: Got It Working
stages.text: Many objects appear and move — created in a counting loop, drawn in a for-each loop.

stages.name: Made It Mine
stages.text: …and I tuned the world: changed the count, size, or speed, added a second list of a different kind (enemies, stars, bubbles), or spawned objects on click.

stages.name: Went Beyond
stages.text: …and I wrote my own environment sprite class (like a `Cloud`) in a new tab and filled the world with it.

thinking: In your own words, in one or two sentences: when do you use a **counting** loop versus a **for-each** loop?

di.h: Motivate the list before you show it
p: Start by writing `coin1`, `coin2`, `coin3` on the board and asking what happens at twelve. Let the tedium land before you offer the fix.
This is the Lesson 5 slot in the arc precisely because students can now *feel* the pain of managing many things. Do not skip straight to the syntax.
"A list is like a bag — you can keep stuffing things in."
Declare, create, add. Show all three on the projector as three separate lines before combining them.

di.h: The two for loops — make this distinction explicit
p: This is the developer note on this lesson and it is the thing to get right.
**Counting loop** (in `setup()`, to CREATE): `for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)`. "`i` counts from 0 to 9 — we use it to repeat the add 10 times."
**For-each loop** (in `draw()`, to VISIT): `for (Blob c : coins)`. "For each coin `c` in the list, move it and draw it."

Both use the word `for`, and in a broad sense both are count-controlled, but they *feel* different: **one counts, one visits.** Students mix them up constantly. Say the distinction out loud more than once, and use the words "create" and "visit" consistently.

di.h: Show the classic mistake on purpose
p: Write `coins.drawSprite();` on the projector and run it. It will not compile.
"The bag is not a coin. You cannot ask the bag to draw itself." Then fix it with the loop. Seeing the error once beats a warning.

di.h: Custom sprite tab (optional, for motivated students)
p: Show the `Cloud` class — there is a working version in `SceneExample/Cloud.pde` in the examples folder.
"It is just like `MyCharacter`, but it draws cloud shapes instead." Same pattern from Lesson 2, no new concept. Students who want a richer world can write their own environment sprites.

guided: Put `coin1`, `coin2`, `coin3` on the board. Ask what happens at twelve. Wait for the groan.
Declare and create the list together. Run — nothing changes, because the list is empty. Name that.
Add the counting loop in `setup()` together. Run — still nothing on screen. Ask why. (They exist, but nothing draws them.)
Add the for-each loop in `draw()`. Run. The world appears. That two-step reveal is worth the extra minute.
As a class, change `12` to `40`, then to `3`. Let them see the loop's power immediately.
Deliberately move the player lines above the coin loop and run. Character vanishes. Move them back. That is draw order, and it sets up Lesson 8.
Release for personalization: colors, counts, a second list, a `mousePressed()` spawner.
pitfalls: **`coins.drawSprite()`** — calling a method on the whole list. The single most common error in this lesson.
**Creating the list but never looping over it in `draw()`.** The objects exist and are invisible. Students think the `add` failed.
**Forgetting `coins = new ArrayList<Blob>();`** — a null pointer exception the moment they call `.add()`.
Mixing the two loop forms: `for (int i = 0; i < coins; i++)` or `for (Blob c : 12)`. Both come from not having the create/visit distinction yet.
Drawing the player **before** the coins, so the character is hidden.
Putting the counting loop in `draw()` — it adds 12 new coins every frame and the sketch grinds to a halt. Dramatic, and a good demo if it happens.
teacher.wrapupAnswer: Counting loop: repeat something a set number of times — used to create. For-each loop: visit every item already in a list — used to move and draw. Accept any wording that separates "create" from "visit."
notes: Use the word "visit" for the for-each loop all period. It gives students language for a distinction they can otherwise only feel.

The `Cloud` class uses `extends Blob`, not `extends Sprite`, so it inherits `collidesWith()`. If students want clouds to be interactive obstacles in Lesson 7, this matters. Do not let a motivated student write `extends Sprite`.
Draw order gets a proper lesson in Lesson 8. Today just plant it.
Fast finishers should write a custom environment sprite rather than adding a third list of plain blobs — it reinforces Lesson 2 and pays off in Lesson 8.
Do not explain generics (`<Blob>`). It is "what kind of bag this is." That is enough.
